Base directory for this skill: /ux/run/work/.claude/skills/metais

# metais

A `.metais` file is a METAIS package: a document template. It declares
the inputs a document needs, each with a JSON Schema and a guide to what
it means, and renders the document from them. The `metais` command reads
it, checks inputs against it and renders it.

## Rules

- **Read a package with `metais`, in place.** Never unzip it, never read
  its raw bytes, never `cat` its README. Every command below takes the
  `.metais` file, or a source directory, as it is.
- **Never invent facts for a real document.** The inputs come from the
  person or from the sources they name. A value nobody supplied is asked
  for, not guessed, and not filled with a placeholder.
- **Fictional data only when the person asks for it** ("example data",
  "sample", "demo", "a preview"). Then generate it with
  `metais render <package> --sample` or `metais sample`; never copy a
  package's examples, and never hand-write placeholder values. An example
  is the author's illustration of the inputs, not the person's data.
- **Follow `next`.** Every command ends with the commands to run next
  (`Next:` in text, `next` in JSON). `<package>`, `<dir>` and `<data dir>`
  there are placeholders for your own paths.

## Filling in and rendering a package

1. `metais inspect report.metais` — what the package is, its guide, every
   input (with the file name it takes in a data directory, such as
   `status.json`), every output, and "Read next". Read all of it. If the
   guide was cut, `metais inspect report.metais --guide`.
2. Run what "Read next" lists, in order:
   - `metais read report.metais <entry>` for each input's meaning document;
   - `metais grep report.metais <pattern> references/` for the references.
3. `metais schema report.metais <input> --fields` — the fields of one
   input, one line each: its pointer (as `--set` takes it), its type,
   `required` or `optional`, its constraints and its title. Read it whole.
   A line that ends `when …` applies only under that condition, such as a
   field another field's value makes required. With no input it lists
   every input's fields; with `--json` they are `result.fields`. Only
   after it, for a field's description, read the whole schema:
   `metais schema report.metais <input>`, or write it to a file with
   `> <input>.schema.json`. Never dig fields out of its `$defs`: the
   listing has already followed every `$ref`.
4. Write a data directory: one file per input, named as `inspect` shows
   (`<input>.json`, `<input>.csv`, …), or one directory per collection
   input. `metais help inputs` explains `--set` and `--inputs-json`, which
   supply values on the command line instead.
5. `metais validate report.metais --data <data dir>` — every finding at
   once. Fix them all and run it again until it is clean.
6. `metais render report.metais --data <data dir> --out <new dir>` — the
   document. `--out` must be a new or empty directory; `--dry-run` lists
   what it would write.

**Fictional data, when asked for:**
`metais render report.metais --sample --out <new dir>` renders an example
of the document from generated data, in one step.
`metais sample report.metais --out <data dir>` writes valid generated data
to start from (`--seed <n>` varies it); then `validate` and `render` as
above. Say in your answer that the data is fictional. Never use generated
data for a real document.

## Writing a package

1. `metais init <dir> --minimal` — a new source directory with one input
   and one template to replace; without `--minimal`, a greeting with an
   example to learn from. Add `--html` for an HTML output: it declares
   `escape: html`, and its template writes data into a `<script>` with
   `json_script`, never `json`.
2. Edit `metais.yaml`, `inputs/`, `templates/` and `examples/`.
   `metais help manifest` gives every field of `metais.yaml` with an
   example; `metais help templates` gives the template language, every
   filter, and escaping, a URL component's `url_encode` included. Preview
   with `metais render <dir> --sample --out <preview dir>`.
3. `metais check <dir>` — every defect, without data.
4. `metais test <dir>` — renders each example and compares it with its
   `expected/` outputs; `metais test <dir> --update` records them.
5. `metais pack <dir>` — check, test, and write `<name>-<version>.metais`.

To change a packed package: `metais unpack report.metais --out <dir>`,
edit, then `check`, `test` and `pack`.

## Machine output

`--json` on any command prints exactly one JSON document on standard
output: `{"format", "ok", "findings", "summary", "result", "next"}`.
`ok` is false when any finding is an error; each finding has a `code`,
a `message` and a `hint`. `metais help json` lists every format.

## When stuck

- `metais help` — the commands and both paths.
- `metais help <command>` — a command's operands, flags, refusals and
  examples.
- `metais help inputs` — supplying inputs, and which source wins.
- `metais help templates` and `metais help manifest` — writing templates
  and `metais.yaml`.
- `metais help refusals <command>` — every code a command can report, with
  the next step.
- A finding's `hint` says what to do; its code is stable.

This skill was installed by `metais skill`. If `metais version` is newer
than the version in the last line, `metais skill --dry-run` says whether to
refresh it.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

Next: metais check — Checks the package, which reports no finding until you edit it. inputs metais.yaml templates numchart/inputs: data.md data.schema.json numchart/templates: page.html.liquid metais: "1.0" name: "numchart" version: "0.1.0" title: "Numchart" description: "Replace this line with what the package produces, in a sentence." guide: |- Replace this guide with what the package produces and what a supplier gives it. Read [what the data means](inputs/data.md) before you supply it. inputs: - name: data title: "Data" schema: inputs/data.schema.json meaning: inputs/data.md forms: - json - yaml outputs: - id: page template: page.html.liquid escape: html metais help templates — Writing templates: the environment, every filter, and escaping. A template is Liquid, in the dialect spec chapter 7 pins. The examples on this page read these inputs: inputs.rows [{"name": "b", "n": 2, "tag": "new"}, {"name": "a", "n": 1, "tag": null}] inputs.note "line 1\nline 2" inputs.title null: declared by the schema, and not supplied A loop over an input, with forloop: {% for row in inputs.rows -%} {{ forloop.index }} of {{ forloop.length }}: {{ row.name }} {% endfor -%} gives 1 of 2: b 2 of 2: a assign, a filter chain, and a test for nil: {% assign names = inputs.rows | map: "name" | sort -%} {% if inputs.title %}{{ inputs.title }}{% else %}Untitled{% endif %} {{ names | join: ", " }} gives Untitled a, b A partial, rendered once per element: templates/row.md holds - {{ row.name }} ({{ row.n }}) and the template {% render "row.md" for inputs.rows as row %} gives - b (2) - a (1) The environment: inputs One member per declared input: its validated value, defaults applied. An optional input not supplied is nil. package The manifest's metais, name, version, title, description, guide, authors, license and homepage, and digest, the package digest. output In a template body: path, the output's path, and root, the relative prefix from its directory to the root of its tree ("", "../", ...). now The render time the caller supplied, in UTC (2026-10-18T09:30:00Z), or nil. It is a template's only clock. sources Where each input came from: origin is file, command-line or default; for a collection, each item's file name, stem and form. item In an output with for_each only: the element being rendered. fan_out Beside item: index, index0, rindex, rindex0, first, last, length, previous and next. Names are strict. A name nothing binds is an error (template.undefined_variable), and so is a property the schema does not declare and the data does not hold (template.undefined_property), never an empty string. A property the schema declares and the data omits is nil, and nil writes nothing. Reading a property of nil is an error (template.nil_property), whatever filter follows, default included; {% if a and a.b %} reads safely. Only nil and false are false: 0, "", [] and {} are true, so {% if inputs.x %} asks whether x was supplied. x == empty holds for an empty string, array or object; x == blank also for nil, false and whitespace. for loops over an array, a range (1..3) or an object, whose members it visits in name order as [name, value] pairs; it takes limit:, offset: and reversed, and else for an empty collection, and break and continue. Inside it, forloop has index and index0 (from 1 and 0), rindex and rindex0 (from the end), first, last, length, parentloop and name. {%- and -%} remove the whitespace before and after a tag; nothing else is trimmed, so a tag alone on its line leaves its line feed. assign binds a value and capture binds the text its block writes, for the rest of the template; neither may take a global's name, forloop or tablerowloop (template.reserved_name). render "" renders a partial: a template under templates/, named by its full path there as a string literal ("parts/row.md"). It takes k: v parameters, with x [as n], or for xs [as n], which renders it once per element and binds forloop. A partial sees its parameters, its own bindings and the globals, and none of its caller's assign, capture or loop variables. include is refused. METAIS adds three tags, whose text is never escaped: embed {% embed "" %} writes an input's bytes exactly as its data-directory file holds them; index: n names an item of a collection. asset {% asset "" %} writes the relative path from the file being rendered to where the render copies an asset under assets/; as: "contents" writes its text, as: "base64" its bytes. provenance {% provenance all %} writes one comment line naming the package, its version and digest, the inputs' digests, the tool and the render time when one was given; name parts to write fewer. Filters: Every filter of the dialect, with an example and what it gives. A filter's keyword argument follows its positional ones: csv: "name", delimiter: ";". In what an example gives, \n is a line feed. Strings: append Adds text at the end. {{ "doc" | append: ".md" }} gives doc.md prepend Adds text at the start. {{ "md" | prepend: "." }} gives .md capitalize Upper-cases the first character and lower-cases the rest. {{ "hELLO" | capitalize }} gives Hello downcase Lower-cases every letter, by Unicode's simple case mapping. {{ "AbC" | downcase }} gives abc upcase Upper-cases every letter, by Unicode's simple case mapping. {{ "abc" | upcase }} gives ABC strip Removes the whitespace at both ends. {{ " a b " | strip }} gives a b lstrip Removes the whitespace at the start. {{ " a " | lstrip | append: "]" }} gives a ] rstrip Removes the whitespace at the end. {{ " a " | rstrip | prepend: "[" }} gives [ a squish Strips both ends and makes each run of whitespace one space. {{ inputs.note | squish }} gives line 1 line 2 strip_html Removes HTML tags. {{ "bold text" | strip_html }} gives bold text strip_newlines Removes every line break. {{ inputs.note | strip_newlines }} gives line 1line 2 newline_to_br Writes
before each line break. {{ inputs.note | newline_to_br }} gives line 1
\nline 2 remove Removes every occurrence of a text. {{ "a-b-c" | remove: "-" }} gives abc remove_first Removes the first occurrence. {{ "a-b-c" | remove_first: "-" }} gives ab-c remove_last Removes the last occurrence. {{ "a-b-c" | remove_last: "-" }} gives a-bc replace Replaces every occurrence of a text with another. {{ "a-b-c" | replace: "-", "+" }} gives a+b+c replace_first Replaces the first occurrence. {{ "a-b-c" | replace_first: "-", "+" }} gives a+b-c replace_last Replaces the last occurrence. {{ "a-b-c" | replace_last: "-", "+" }} gives a-b+c split Splits a string into an array at each separator. {{ "a,b,c" | split: "," | join: " " }} gives a b c truncate Cuts a string to a number of characters, the ellipsis (... unless given) included. {{ "abcdefgh" | truncate: 6 }} gives abc... truncatewords Keeps a number of words, then the ellipsis (... unless given). {{ "one two three" | truncatewords: 2 }} gives one two... Numbers (integers give an integer): abs The absolute value. {{ -3 | abs }} gives 3 ceil Rounds up to an integer. {{ 1.2 | ceil }} gives 2 floor Rounds down to an integer. {{ 1.8 | floor }} gives 1 round Rounds half away from zero, to a number of decimal places when given. {{ 2.5 | round }} gives 3 plus Adds; a float adds as the decimal it is written as. {{ 0.1 | plus: 0.2 }} gives 0.3 minus Subtracts. {{ 5 | minus: 7 }} gives -2 times Multiplies. {{ 3 | times: 1.5 }} gives 4.5

input.content:
# Data

- **title** is the page heading and names what the numbers measure.
- **unit** (optional) is what one number counts, such as `ms` or `orders`.
  It appears in the tooltip and the table header.
- **values** is the list of numbers to chart, in plotting order. Each is
  one point on a line chart, numbered from 1 by its position. The list is
  written into a JavaScript array in the page, and the page shows a table
  of the same numbers beneath the chart. Take the numbers from the person
  or their source; do not make any up.

    - name: Example Docs Team
      email: docs@example.org
      url: https://example.org/docs
  license: Apache-2.0
  homepage: https://example.org/release-notes
  inputs:
    - name: release
      title: The release
      schema: inputs/release.schema.json
    - name: changes
      title: The changes in the release
      description: One change per row, newest first.
      schema: inputs/changes.schema.json
      meaning: inputs/changes.md
      forms: [json, yaml, csv]
      csv:
        delimiter: ";"
  outputs:
    - id: notes
      template: notes.md.liquid
    - id: page
      template: page.html.liquid

The same package's outputs could instead write one page per change with
for_each, and a zip holding a template, an asset and a mirror:

  outputs:
    - id: change_pages
      template: change.md.liquid
      for_each: inputs.changes
      when: item.public
      path: "changes/{{ item.id }}.md"
    - id: bundle
      path: "release-{{ inputs.release.version }}.zip"
      container:
        format: zip
        entries:
          - template: notes.md.liquid
            path: README.md
            first: true
          - asset: logo.png
            path: images/logo.png

content.text:
I made the package: `numchart/numchart-0.1.0.metais`. It passes `metais check` and `metais test`, and the rendered page puts the numbers into a JavaScript array.

I haven't opened a rendered page in a browser, so the chart's layout and hover tooltip are untested. I did read the generated HTML, which shows `const values = [12,19,3,5,2,25,14.5];` for the example data.

**Inputs**
- `title` (required) is the page heading.
- `values` (required) is the list of numbers, at least one and at most 5000.
- `unit` (optional) is a label such as `ms` or `orders`, shown in the tooltip and the table header.

**What the page does**
- **Array:** the template writes `values` and `unit` into `<script>` using `json_script`. The numbers can't break out of the script, and a title containing `</script>` stays harmless.
- **Chart:** an SVG line chart with the numbers plotted in order and numbered from 1. It has a hover crosshair and tooltip, a "Table of values" section, and light and dark colors that follow the system setting.
- **Styling:** it uses one blue series color from the dataviz palette. I didn't run the palette validator, since one series has no pair of colors to compare.

**How to use it**
Run `metais render numchart-0.1.0.metais --data <dir> --out <new dir>`. The data directory holds a `data.json` with `title`, `values` and optionally `unit`. I didn't have your numbers, so the only values in the package are the invented ones in `examples/basic/inputs/data.json`. `metais test` needs that example, so it ships in the package.
